claim: The particles in the bottle in use fluoresce under Aura3 green excitation and are visible through the 605 band of the emission filter wheel. This establishes that their emission overlaps the bands this optical path uses; it is not a spectral peak.

numbers.name: path_excitation_band_nominal_centre
numbers.note: the NOMINAL CENTRE of an instrument band, not a property of the particle. Observed through filters, not on a spectrometer. Precision is declared coarse on purpose (5.8): a band observation is not an nm-level statement about a spectrum.

numbers.name: path_emission_band_nominal_centre
numbers.note: as above. A6 needs the wavelength the path actually collects; this is the band that was used for the observation, which is close to but not the same claim, and the single-band filter that defines it is an open gap.

valid_until.event: the emission filter wheel, the cube in the turret, or the excitation light engine is changed. BOTH the date and the event are set, and the event is the one that actually invalidates this: a ten-year date alone would say the observation still holds the day after somebody swaps the filter wheel, which is the single change that certainly breaks it. The date is an outer bound, not the condition

validity_conditions: WHAT THIS ESTABLISHES IS COMPATIBILITY, NOT A SPECTRUM. Observed through filters rather than on a spectrometer, so the claim is that whatever is in the bottle emits into the bands this path uses. 555 and 605 are nominal centres of instrument bands and are NOT the particle's excitation and emission peaks. Writing them as peaks would manufacture spectral precision nobody measured -- and A1 will later need the overlap between a spectrum and a passband, a calculation that a band centre recorded as a peak makes look possible when it is not. THE DATE 2026-09-19 IS ASSIGNED FOR CONVENIENCE and was not stated as the date of observation; it is when the fact reached this store. For a configuration-dependent observation that distinction can matter and this entry cannot answer it. THE CAL ID WAS MINTED HERE, not supplied by the person. Identifiers belong to their owner and this store owns this one; it must not be read back to them as something they said. IT DOES NOT GIVE A6 ITS WAVELENGTH, AND HALF OF WHY IS NOW ANSWERED. The cube in the turret is MULTIBAND, so its marking does not name what the path collects; the single-band filters sit in the emission wheel. WHICH FILTER was an open gap when this was written and is no longer: asked directly on 2026-09-20, the person said the 605 band is this bench's name for the FF01-595/31-32 filter, which is red_path_605_is_the_ff01_595_31_filter at E5. So the designated centre of the band this observation was made through is 595 with a 31 nm width (filter_ff01_595_31_32_passband, E3), and 605 is a local name for the path rather than a measured band. WHICH POSITION carries it is still not recorded -- emission_wheel_camera_mapping is `operator_recall:` at E5 and says `probably` -- and the identification itself is a recall rather than a reading, so both close the same way: by opening the wheel and reading the designation, which would be `operator_read:` at E3. This entry remains the observation that the particles are visible on the path, not a measurement of the path. The numbers here are still the wheel's nominal band centres and still are not the particle's peaks. WHAT IT DOES DO IS REFUTE THE PRODUCT IDENTIFICATION. A particle emitting at 680 nm, as the Abvigen sheet specifies, does not light up under green excitation and show through a 605 band. The observation was made on this bench and the specification was not, so the specification loses -- 10.3 rule 1, a run elsewhere is not a run here, which binds a vendor exactly as it binds a prior project. See bottle_label_states_no_product for why that cannot be settled by looking. `validity` PINS THE BANDS AS POINTS, AND THAT IS A CONFIGURATION IDENTITY RATHER THAN A SPECTRAL WIDTH. The schema requires a non-empty condition range from any `calibration:` source, and the reason it gives is exact: an unbounded calibration is a measurement with no event, which is the same claim an operator could have made from memory. The only conditions honestly available here are which bands were in the path, so those are what is pinned -- at their nominal centres, as points, because no bandwidth was measured and inventing one to fill an interval would be the over-claim this field exists to prevent. A query at any other band therefore comes back `disjoint`, which is the correct answer: this observation says nothing about a path it was not made on. What is genuinely unmatchable is the rest of the configuration -- this cube, this wheel, this light engine -- which has no quantity-to-interval shape at all and lives in `valid_until.event`. Third case of that limit after 'at the generator' on the trapping laser and 'the room' on the ambient temperature; raised with manager-librarian as one problem rather than three. IT HAS A SUBJECT NOW. This entry carried none because check 44 rightly refused one -- there was no registry a sample resolved against, and an id was not invented to make it pass. `samples.v0.json` now exists and `subject.kind` takes `sample` (a675c4e), wired to resolve against that table and nothing else. The refusal is what produced the registry: a check rejecting the honest form of an assertion is the strongest evidence that the thing being asserted had nowhere to live. THIS ENTRY REFUTES TWO OTHERS, AND SAYS SO IN A FIELD RATHER THAN IN PROSE. It carried `conflict_with` on those two until 1837ecd gave refutation its own field. The difference is not bookkeeping: `kb_conflicts` was returning the pair and telling the caller to decide by conditions, when there are no conditions under which a particle emitting at 680 nm shows through a 605 band under green excitation. `DISPROVED` had been stated only inside four thousand characters of prose, which is not a place a caller reads. Found by librarian-agent-a5 running kb_conflicts instead of reading the entries.
